paper.title: Cortex-wide single-cell activity mapping in freely moving mice
paper.abstract: How the cortex supports complex, naturalistic behavior can be revealed only in freely moving animals. Although head-mounted microscopes promise access to the neural dynamics underlying such behavior, fundamental trade-offs among field of view, spatial resolution, device weight, and background contamination have prevented cortex-wide single-neuron recording, leaving distributed cortical coordination largely inaccessible. To meet these challenges, we introduce COMET (Cortex-wide Observational Miniature Epifluorescence Technique), a 3.75-g head-mounted mesoscope that integrates an aberration-controlled wide-field optical design, uniform high-efficiency excitation and single-coaxial power-and-data transmission with an end-to-end denoising and signal-extraction pipeline. This enables cortex-wide calcium imaging at single-cell resolution in freely moving mice. COMET captures activity from >15,000 layer 2/3 neurons per 5-min recording over fields of view up to 10 mm in diameter while preserving natural behavior. Benchmarking against benchtop two-photon microscopy demonstrates high spatial concordance of detected neurons and matched event-level calcium dynamics. We apply COMET to social interaction to quantify region-specific engagement and to an auditory trace fear-conditioning task that requires natural movement and behavioral expression, revealing time-ordered changes in regional firing-rate structure and functional connectivity preceding a global conditioned response. COMET provides an open, lightweight hardware-software framework for linking single-neuron activity to cortex-scale network dynamics during freely expressed behaviors under changing internal or external conditions.

paper.title: A disinhibition-based model of CA1 place field sequences
paper.abstract: Because of the paucity of pattern-generating recurrent excitation in the CA1 hippocampal region, place field sequences are assumed to be inherited from upstream regions. Alternatively, disinhibition may play a role in shaping pyramidal cell activity. We propose a model of CA1 activity using one layer of excitatory cells and one layer of inhibitory cells, with local excitatory-to-inhibitory connectivity, broad inhibitory-to-excitatory connectivity without recurrent excitatory connections, and broad inhibitory-inhibitory connections. The layers need not follow a topographic organization; instead they can represent sequences of place cells structured by local inhibition. Our mathematical model of CA1 neurons with data-inspired connectivity demonstrates place fields sharpened by disinhibition, mimicking a recently discovered decrease in inhibitory input within place fields and matching in vivo patterns of disinhibition. Mathematical analysis of our model suggests the importance of inhibitory-to-excitatory connections in control of place cell firing rate and sparsity. We also demonstrate that a disinhibition-based mechanism of pattern generation is more flexible without recurrent excitation than the recurrent excitation-rich CA3-like model. Finally, we demonstrate disinhibition as an efficient mechanism for internally-generated sequential activity, where the speed of sequential change depends on both input strength and inhibitory-to-excitatory connection strength. Overall, our model suggests that theta time-scale disinhibition is a foundational mechanism of self-organized sequential activity in the CA1 region, and, possibly, in other networks.

paper.title: Operator-valued free probability applied to recurrent neural networks with heterogeneity in local and global circuit structures
paper.abstract: Random connectivity is a common assumption in models of recurrent neural networks, yet biological circuits combine heterogeneous synaptic connections with organization into distinct anatomical regions and functional groups. How does this global structure interact with cellular and local circuit heterogeneity to shape the dimensionality of population activity? In our work, we use operator-valued free probability to derive the covariance spectrum and effective dimension of recurrent networks with heterogeneous gains and block-structured random connectivity. This framework handles the noncommuting matrix operations through which cellular and circuit heterogeneity jointly determine population variability. We show that the linear relationship between effective dimension and firing rate uniformity persists despite global connectivity structure. At fixed total connectivity variance and with identical firing rate distributions across areas, concentrating variance within one area decreases dimension, whereas concentrating it in directed connections between areas increases dimension. Together, these results establish a mechanistic connection between circuit organization and population dimensionality, and demonstrate how operator-valued free probability unifies cellular, local, and global sources of heterogeneity in recurrent networks.
